agent: Claude Code (CLAUDE.md, this repository) — WP-03a Fault 2: GATE kind INPUT validates but cannot run
summary_for_principal:
You asked me to fix the second bug: a workflow step that gathers an answer from someone (an "INPUT" gate) passes every check when written, then crashes with a confusing error the moment anyone runs it. The work package gave me two choices: build real support, or refuse it cleanly up front instead. I chose to refuse it, and proved the fix with tests.

Why refuse rather than build: building this properly needs three genuine design decisions only a product call can settle — which reviewers (automated policy, AI, or a person) may answer this kind of gate; what shape an AI reviewer's answer must take; and how a person actually submits their answer. None are written down anywhere, and guessing risks building the wrong thing. They're written up plainly in the technical record for whenever you want that work done.

What changed: authoring this kind of gate is now refused immediately with a clear reason, instead of passing checks and failing confusingly later. Full suite: 346 tests passing.

Numbered actions:
1. Nothing needs deciding right now — I made the call the work package authorized.
2. Opinion: when you want real support for this, the three open questions above are what to resolve first.

interpretation.ask_as_given: FAULT 2 — INPUT gates validate but cannot run. A GATE with kind: INPUT, answer_type, answer_into and on: { ANSWERED: ... } passes validation (validate.py:786 accepts INPUT) and then dies at runtime with "gate 'x': no route declared for verdict 'PERMIT'" -> ending FAILED, because _advance_gate never reads node.kind, answer_type, answer_into or ANSWERED. Implement INPUT gates per spec §7.6 (the answer is written through answer_into and routed on ANSWERED; INDETERMINATE passes on as for APPROVAL), or, if you judge that too large for this pass, make the validator refuse INPUT until the engine supports it — do not leave the silent path. Say which you chose and why. One PR per fault, tests first, spec silence goes to a proposed spec change not a code guess, two-channel reporting per PR, stop after each PR and report the link before starting the next.
interpretation.read_as: Decide between the two named options and commit to one, rather than partially implementing or leaving the crash in place; if refusing, do it at both the validator and the engine (since the validator is advisory), and if the spec is silent on details a real implementation would need, name those gaps explicitly rather than guessing at them in code.

filled_in.gap: The work package left the implement-vs-refuse choice to my own judgement ('if you judge that too large').
filled_in.assumed: Refuse, not implement. Tracing what a real implementation needs surfaced three genuinely unspecified design questions (which decider kinds may answer an INPUT gate, given PolicyPort has no channel for a typed answer; what output shape an agent decider's Tool must return, given decision@1 has no field for one; how a person submits an answer at all, given decide()'s public signature only accepts an ADR-028 verdict) — each would need either a PolicyPort/API change or a guessed answer. Guessing at any of them would be exactly the 'invent a rule in code where the spec is silent' CLAUDE.md asks me not to do; refusing cleanly avoids inventing anything while still closing the actual reported bug (the confusing runtime crash).
filled_in.grounded_in: CLAUDE.md: 'If the spec is silent or wrong, do not invent a rule in code: write the gap as a proposed spec change in your PR and flag it in the run record' — applied directly, since all three gaps are the spec (§7.6) being silent, not an implementation detail I could reasonably infer.

options_rejected: Implement INPUT gates per spec §7.6: rejected for this pass — §7.6's own text is one sentence and does not say which decider kinds may answer an INPUT gate (PolicyPort's evaluate_policy has no field for a typed answer), what output shape an agent decider's Tool must return (decision@1 has nowhere to carry one), or how a person submits an answer at all (decide()'s public signature only accepts an ADR-028 verdict, and §12.1 names no fourth call). Guessing at any of these would invent unauthorised schema/API surface rather than follow the spec.

lessons.maxim: When a work package offers 'implement it, or refuse it if implementing is too large' as an explicit choice, trace what a real implementation would actually need BEFORE picking — the tracing itself is what tells you whether the size problem is effort (a reason to just build it) or unresolved design (a reason to refuse and name the gaps), and the two calls need different justifications.
lessons.incident: Tracing a real INPUT-gate implementation surfaced three genuinely unspecified design questions in the space of a few minutes, each blocking on a spec clarification or a port/API change rather than on engineering effort — confirming refuse-and-name-the-gaps was the right call here, not a shortcut. Writing that reasoning down (rather than just asserting 'too large') is what makes the choice auditable and gives the principal something concrete to commission later.
lessons.destination: docs/spec/process-definition.md's own D26 entry carries this reasoning directly, as the artefact this lesson changed.
lessons.proposed_check: Before choosing 'refuse, too large to implement' on any future gap, write out the concrete blocking questions a real implementation would hit, the same way D26 does — if none surface, effort alone is not sufficient grounds to refuse rather than build.
